Meanwhile, Fury will not face criminal charges from Greater Manchester Police (GMP) regarding alleged homophobic remarks. GMP received a complaint about his statements on the BBC's Victoria Derbyshire programme but classified them as a "hate incident" rather than a "hate crime."

Making me a good cup of tea, that's what I believe." The new world champion had also previously claimed that the legalisation of paedophilia, alongside the decriminalisation of homosexuality and abortion, would signal "the devil come home." Subsequently, the Manchester-born fighter clarified, "Tyson Fury loves his fellow humans. He doesn't hate anybody."

Greg Rutherford, a fellow nominee for BBC Sports Personality of the Year and a long jump champion, initially intended to withdraw from the event due to Fury's comments but later changed his mind. Furthermore, Fury, who captured the WBA, IBF, and WBO titles on November 28 by defeating Klitschko, was stripped of his IBF belt on Tuesday. This occurred because he opted for a rematch with Klitschko instead of fulfilling the IBF's mandatory defence against Ukrainian Vyacheslav Glazkov.

West Yorkshire Police recently admitted that 16,000 parking fines issued by their Police Community Support Officers (PCSOs) were invalid due to an "administrative error." However, the police stated that there were no legal grounds for issuing refunds, as such payments would have to come from public funds. A significant number of drivers paid these fines without questioning their legality. Following a review of PCSO authority in March, it was discovered that some PCSOs, who had joined the force years prior, had not been properly authorised to issue parking tickets from the outset. Police acknowledged in a statement that "an administrative error rendered the authorisation invalid." The force's records, accessible back to 2006, revealed that 16,000 tickets were impacted, leading to a total of £485,000 being paid into the courts. The force also conceded that other fines might have been issued under similar incorrect circumstances up to three years earlier. They confirmed seeking legal counsel on the issue. A spokesperson explained that, after legal assessment, they are confident there are no legal grounds for refunds, which would otherwise use public money. The core reasoning is that drivers had the opportunity to dispute the tickets' validity in court at the time, and penalties were only imposed on those found guilty. By choosing to pay the fine, motorists effectively accepted responsibility for the offence and forfeited their right to challenge it legally. The police confirmed that this "anomaly" has since been rectified, and PCSOs now possess the full authority to issue such fines.

Lord Advocate Frank Mulholland informed Scottish Parliament members that a fatal accident inquiry would be convened regarding the death of Sheku Bayoh. Mr. Bayoh, 31, died on May 3 in police custody following an incident in Kirkcaldy. His family expressed welcome for the announcement, hoping the Lord Advocate would indeed establish the complete truth of what transpired.

Mr. Mulholland also conveyed to MSPs that additional work was still necessary from the Police Investigations and Review Commissioner (Pirc), particularly concerning the cause of death, before the overall inquiry could be finalized. He remarked on the profound impact of this tragedy on the family, having met them twice, noting their remarkable dignity in coping with their loss. He asserted they were justified in demanding answers, and that a thorough, impartial, and objective investigation was their due. Mulholland expressed confidence that this process could be conducted swiftly without compromising its comprehensiveness.

He further clarified that a fatal accident inquiry would proceed irrespective of any decisions regarding criminal proceedings, specifically because Mr. Bayoh had died while in detention. Mulholland explained that such an inquiry would permit all relevant evidence to be presented in a public court, open to both the public and media. This evidence would be rigorously scrutinized by all involved parties, including the family, enabling the Sheriff to make factual findings and recommendations concerning Mr. Bayoh's death in a judgment accessible to everyone.

Aamer Anwar, the solicitor representing Mr. Bayoh's family, commented that while the family always anticipated an FAI, they do not currently consider it a full resolution for Sheku Bayoh's death in custody. Anwar described an FAI as essentially the absolute minimum measure, adding that predicting the outcome of the investigations at this point would be premature, especially if they prove genuinely robust and impartial. He highlighted that nearly five months had passed since Sheku's death, and the family's hope was that the Lord Advocate could deliver the truth of what occurred, recognizing that true justice cannot be achieved without it.

Two charities, Mencap and the Challenging Behaviour Foundation, have highlighted the dangers associated with relocating patients great distances from their homes. This caution coincides with the imminent release of findings from a serious case review concerning patient abuse at a private facility located close to Bristol. The BBC Panorama programme brought this abuse to light through covert filming. Eleven individuals have pleaded guilty to charges of neglect and mistreatment linked to the incidents. The South Gloucestershire Safeguarding Adults Board (SAB) commissioned an independent expert to conduct this review.

Since the Panorama broadcast in May of the previous year, Mencap and the Challenging Behaviour Foundation have received 260 reports from families detailing abuse and neglect within institutional care settings. Their collaborative report, titled 'Out of Sight', documented numerous severe incidents reported by families, encompassing physical and sexual assault, along with excessive use of restraint.

Mark Goldring, Mencap's chief executive, expressed concern, stating that without a robust government plan to shut down large care facilities and establish suitable local services for individuals with learning disabilities, another scandal akin to Winterbourne View is highly probable. The charities indicated that hundreds of people with learning disabilities are presently housed in assessment and treatment units similar to Winterbourne View. They highlighted that many of these facilities are situated far from patients' homes, increasing their vulnerability to neglect and abuse.

Vivien Cooper, who founded the Challenging Behaviour Foundation, voiced profound worries regarding patient safety and well-being. She elaborated that "hundreds of individuals with learning disabilities are being placed in distant care institutions, often for years unnecessarily, leaving them susceptible to neglect and abuse."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health affirmed their stance: individuals should, whenever feasible, receive support to reside in their own homes within their local communities. While acknowledging that a limited number of cases may necessitate high-quality assessment and treatment services, potentially involving brief inpatient stays, they stressed that this should not replace excellent community-based care. The spokesperson underlined the critical importance of properly commissioning and regularly reviewing all services, ensuring they are not employed as permanent solutions.

Subsequent to the BBC investigation, twenty-four patients were moved from the Castlebeck-operated Winterbourne View hospital, located near Hambrook. The facility closed the subsequent month. American Troy Bradley and Russian Leonid Tiukhtyaev successfully landed their Two Eagles Balloon, their team announced. They asserted that they had broken world records for distance and duration, having flown for over 137 hours and traveled more than 5,209 miles (8,383km). To officially set new records, the team was required to exceed existing benchmarks by one percent.

In a statement, the Two Eagles team confirmed the balloon's safe descent offshore near La Poza Grande, along the Baja coast. The pilots skillfully guided the craft to a gentle water landing approximately four miles off the Baja coast. The balloon remained stable and inflated, and both pilots were reported to be in good condition.

Their journey commenced in Japan on Sunday, with an initial goal of landing in Canada or the United States. However, unfavorable weather conditions compelled them to alter their trajectory towards Mexico. A Mexican fishing boat subsequently met them at sea.

The statement underscored that a sea landing was permissible according to international rules governing world record establishment. It noted that previous around-the-world attempts, using different balloon types, also concluded with water landings and were validated as records. To surpass the 1981 records by the required one percent, the pilots needed to remain airborne for approximately 138 hours and 45 minutes for duration, and cover around 5,260 miles for distance. The Two Eagles Balloon team specified their landing occurred after "six days, 16 hours and 37 minutes," having covered a remarkable 6,646 miles.

Navigating gas-air balloons proves difficult, as their movement depends on harnessing varying wind speeds and directions at different altitudes. To adjust height, pilots possess only a helium release valve for descent and sandbags to jettison for ascent.

The advanced "Two Eagles" balloon, constructed from a robust Kevlar and carbon-fibre composite, remarkably weighs only 220 pounds (100kg). It is equipped with monitors and other instruments that meticulously track their flight path and collect data for submission to record-keeping authorities. The specially engineered capsule, positioned beneath a massive helium-filled envelope, is designed for flights lasting up to ten days. Within this craft, the pilots occupy a confined, low-ceilinged living space.

In the aftermath, four men were sentenced to 18 to 30 years in prison, with an additional seven individuals (men and women) receiving jail terms of four to six years. Testimony revealed the confrontation took place near Curuguaty, in eastern Paraguay's Canindeyu province. Approximately 250 riot police were dispatched to clear about 70 subsistence farmers from a Campos Morumbi agricultural company property. The farmers had been occupying the land to advocate for agrarian reform.

Notably, the Paraguayan prosecution service failed to investigate the farmers' deaths, and both local and international human rights organizations raised concerns about judicial irregularities throughout the trial. Furthermore, five of the defendants undertook a hunger strike lasting over 30 days.

Unequal land ownership has historically fueled violent conflicts in Paraguay. A 2008 census highlighted this disparity: a mere 2.6% of landowners control 85.5% of the country's land, while 91.4% of small farmers (with holdings under 20 hectares) possess only 6% of agricultural land. Advocates for agrarian reform largely attribute this imbalance to major agricultural conglomerates specializing in soy exports. The Curuguaty incident then served as the catalyst for the opposition Colorado Party to initiate impeachment proceedings against President Lugo, holding him responsible for the fatalities.

According to PwC's yearly survey, only 37% of respondents anticipate economic improvement in 2015, a decrease from 44% in the previous year. Unsurprisingly, Russian executives, once the most optimistic, are now the least so, a shift attributed to sanctions and declining oil prices. In the United Kingdom, there has been a significant increase in apprehension regarding talent availability. The percentage of CEOs in the UK worried about skill shortages jumped from 64% last year to 84% this year, a rate significantly exceeding that in Germany, France, or Spain. This escalating concern is partly attributed to the UK's high employment rates, which reduce the available talent pool, and partly to worries about the quality of the education system. Globally, the primary concerns for chief executives include geopolitical instability, excessive regulation, and cyber security threats. The report, unveiled at the World Economic Forum in Davos, highlighted that apprehension concerning cyber threats has risen more than any other issue since last year, noting that recent attacks on gaming and entertainment networks are expected to further elevate this perceived risk. Dennis Nally, PwC's chairman, commented that CEO confidence has significantly declined in oil-producing countries globally, primarily due to collapsing crude oil prices. He cited Russian CEOs as a prime example, shifting from being the most confident in the prior year's survey to the least confident this year. Nally added that executives in the Middle East, Venezuela, and Nigeria have also experienced a drop in confidence. Furthermore, he observed a noticeable transfer of confidence from emerging markets towards Western economies. For the upcoming year, chief executives identified the United States as their top market for growth, surpassing China for the first time since this question was introduced five years ago. PwC conducted this survey by interviewing over 1,300 chief executives across 77 nations during the last quarter of 2014.

Star Randel-Hanson murdered 70-year-old Derick Marney at a Brighton apartment in Vernon Terrace during May 2015. Ten days later, on the Brighton seafront, Randel-Hanson confessed to the crime in a tearful breakdown while consulting tarot reader Jayne Braiden. Ms. Braiden informed the police, but the call was deemed a "non-emergency," leading her to wait an hour with the murderer for an officer's arrival.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Ms. Braiden recounted that Randel-Hanson became emotional and cried as they reached the 'devil card' during the reading. She described the situation as a "shock" and her first encounter with a murder confession, emphasizing the need for professionalism to keep him calm. Mr. Marney's death resulted from a six-inch (15cm) stab wound to his side, which had perforated vital organs. Sussex Police stated that Randel-Hanson's motive for the murder remained "unclear." He was subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment on May 9.

After establishing trust, Ms. Braiden sought his permission to step outside and contact the police, which he granted. She recounted explaining to the 999 operator that she was a tarot reader and a man had just confessed to murder. However, she was informed it was a non-priority matter and advised to dial the non-emergency line. She expressed unsurprising disappointment that they didn't believe her initially. Subsequently, she purchased a drink for Randel-Hanson from an adjacent shop, and they waited together for 55 minutes for officers to appear.

Ms. Braiden also gained his consent to take notes, recording details such as names, locations, the stabbing site, and the body's whereabouts. She deliberately avoided asking for his motive, sensing his reluctance to discuss it. Intriguingly, they even shared a joke about the police's delayed arrival. Nevertheless, Randel-Hanson grew tense as both of them vigilantly watched through the glass doors for the police. Sussex Police later acknowledged that the call had been incorrectly prioritized. A spokesperson confirmed the incident was discussed with the relevant call handler, and "appropriate guidance was provided."

Glenfield Hospital's East Midlands Congenital Heart Centre is set to discontinue its children's surgical services, an announcement made on Wednesday. This decision stems from a national review of ten units, aiming to consolidate specialist expertise into fewer locations. The charity Heartlink swiftly expressed its opposition to this judgement. John Rigby, a Heartlink spokesman, stated their intention to "take stock, listen to what our reps have to say and be guided by them," vowing to "fight to do our very best to keep children's services here [at Glenfield]."

Annually, the centre performs around 230 operations on children and 70 on adults. It also boasts the UK's largest ECMO unit, which provides partial cardiopulmonary bypass to oxygenate the blood of critically ill patients. Although pediatric surgeries will cease, the unit will remain open for patient diagnosis, monitoring, and non-surgical treatments.

Serving a population of approximately five million, the centre's closure means the next comparable facility is in Birmingham, roughly 40 miles (64.4 km) away. Leslie Hamilton, vice-chair of the Safe and Sustainable review's steering group, articulated the surgical community's concern that expertise was too thinly spread across the country. He explained the rationale for consolidation: "We felt we had to concentrate the expertise and reduce the number of centres in the country so we could have bigger centres with bigger surgical teams. That would lead to sustainable care for the future and also a big improvement in care."

Tony Fowlston's three-year-old son, Lewis, has been a patient at Glenfield. The family regularly travels about 60 miles (96.5 km) from Boston, Lincolnshire, to access specialists. Mr. Fowlston highlighted that further travel could pose a serious risk, given Lewis recently suffered a cardiac arrest shortly after arriving at Glenfield. He critically questioned the alternative: "He could have had that cardiac arrest on the way to, say, Birmingham. Could he have had the same service in the back of an ambulance? I very much doubt it." Campaign group Liberty asserts that the extensive collection of electronic data by intelligence agencies, facilitated by certain powers, constitutes an "assault on our freedom." The Investigatory Powers Act (IPA), which grants these powers, received royal assent in November. The government has pledged to uphold this legislation.

Under the IPA, state agencies are authorized to control and alter electronic devices, access private communications like texts, online messages, and emails, and monitor phone calls, even without any suspicion of criminal activity. The act requires telecommunication firms to store metadata—including sender, location, and time—for calls, emails, texts, and web browsing, but explicitly not the content itself.

Liberty, however, seeks to legally contest the legitimacy of these powers and is publicly fundraising for a judicial review. Liberty director Martha Spurrier states that the government, last year, "exploited fear and distraction to quietly create the most extreme surveillance regime of any democracy in history." She added that "hundreds of thousands" have since called for its repeal, deeming it an "unprecedented, unjustified assault on our freedom." In November 2016, a petition advocating the act's repeal garnered over 118,000 signatures.

The Investigatory Powers Act, proposed by then-Home Secretary Theresa May, was approved by the House of Lords on November 19. Though the act's "bulk powers" are highly contentious, security services and the government maintain they are vital for counter-terrorism. Last month, demands arose for the government to revise the act after the European Court of Justice ruled "general and indiscriminate" retention of communications data unlawful. EU judges stipulated such data could only be retained for serious crime investigations. BBC legal correspondent Clive Coleman noted the government's strong commitment to defending the act, asserting it protects both privacy and security, received unprecedented parliamentary scrutiny, and secured cross-party support.

His manager, Barry McGuigan, hailed Taylor as "very special," stressing the importance of selecting opponents carefully and at the right moment.

The Hungarian opponent, Mate, entered the contest with an impressive record of 17 wins from 22 previous fights. However, it was immediately clear that Taylor was far superior. Taylor charged from his corner, sending Mate to the canvas within just 45 seconds. A subsequent left hook from the Commonwealth Games champion floored Mate once more, prompting the referee to intervene and stop the fight after only 85 seconds of the first round, sparing Mate from further punishment.

Taylor admitted he was taken aback by the swift victory, having anticipated a more challenging bout in front of his home crowd. He commented on the hostile atmosphere, sensing Mate's apprehension in the ring and his own superior power.

McGuigan, a former world champion, remarked that the fight offered little new insight into his boxer's abilities. He described it as a "pretty unproductive exercise" since Taylor didn't get the expected number of rounds, but reaffirmed Taylor's formidable punching power, noting Mate's inability to recover from the knockdown.

Moving forward, McGuigan stated a tougher opponent would be sought for Taylor's next contest. He acknowledged Taylor's high skill level and stressed the need to find opponents of even higher caliber. Taylor, meanwhile, plans to return to the ring before the end of the year, deferring any potential title fights for the time being. A study published in the Journal of Aesthetic Nursing reveals a rising inclination among individuals under 25 to receive anti-wrinkle injections. However, the findings indicate that such "frozen faces" might impede young people's ability to fully develop emotional expression. A prominent UK plastic surgery association deems the cosmetic use of Botox in teenagers to be "morally wrong." Botox, and similar neurotoxins, function by temporarily immobilizing muscles in the upper facial region, thereby diminishing wrinkles that appear during frowning.

Helen Collier, the nurse practitioner who conducted this research, attributes young people's aspiration for an "inexpressive frozen face" to the influence of reality television and celebrity culture. She highlights the widely recognized psychological concept of the facial feedback hypothesis, which posits that adolescents acquire social interaction skills by imitating others' facial expressions. Collier states that "our capacity as human beings to exhibit a broad spectrum of emotions is highly reliant on facial expressions." She adds that "emotions like empathy and sympathy are vital for our survival and for developing into self-assured, communicative adults." Nevertheless, she cautions that an increasing number of young individuals with "blank-faced" appearances might impair their capability to accurately express feelings. She warns, "Eliminating these expressions could impede their emotional and social maturation."

The study advocates for medical professionals to employ assessment instruments to determine if there are clear clinical justifications for administering Botox. While various assessment scales exist, evaluating factors such as skin thickness, sun damage, and wrinkle depth, experts caution that certain Botox clinics prioritize financial profit over patient well-being. Ms. Collier encourages therapists to devote time to enhancing young people's self-confidence instead of resorting to injections. She further states that "although the majority of the toxin's effects are temporary, studies indicate that muscles may not fully recover from the injections." She stresses, "It is crucial to comprehend the repercussions of initiating treatments at too young an age."

Dr. Michael Lewis, a psychology researcher at Cardiff University, explains that "the expressions we form on our faces influence the emotions we experience." He elaborates, "We smile due to happiness, yet smiling also generates happiness." He concludes that "medications like Botox inhibit a patient's ability to create specific expressions, potentially impacting our natural process of learning to feel emotions." Rajiv Grover, president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, asserts that "administering Botox to teenagers for cosmetic reasons is ethically indefensible and something no responsible practitioner would undertake." He warns, "This practice can only intensify body image concerns during a sensitive developmental period." Ms. Collier's findings are scheduled to be presented at the Clinical Cosmetic and Reconstructive Expo in October.

A six-year study followed over 200,000 Australians, both smokers and non-smokers aged 45 and older. BMC Medicine reported that the risk of death increased proportionally with cigarette consumption. Daily consumption of 10 cigarettes doubled this risk, and those smoking 20 cigarettes daily faced a four to five times greater likelihood of death. While a smoker might live a long life, their habit significantly reduces this probability. Smoking is known to elevate the risk of numerous health issues, such as heart disease and various cancers.

Cancer Research UK currently estimates that 50% of long-term smokers ultimately succumb to cancer or other diseases linked to smoking. However, more recent data indicates this proportion could be greater. Professor Emily Banks, the lead researcher of the Australian study, noted that newer investigations involving UK women, British physicians, and American Cancer Society volunteers have indicated the figure could be as high as 67%.

Banks commented that while the detrimental effects of smoking were known, their study provided direct, independent evidence corroborating concerning international trends. She added that despite Australia's low smoking rates, their research showed smokers faced approximately three times the risk of premature death compared to non-smokers, and were projected to die about 10 years sooner. George Butterworth, Cancer Research UK's tobacco policy manager, expressed significant worry that the adverse impact of smoking might be more severe than previously understood.

Butterworth noted that previous UK studies conservatively estimated that one in two long-term smokers die from smoking-related conditions, but the new Australian data suggested a higher risk. He cautioned that due to differences in smoking habits between Australia and the UK, such as consumption levels and starting age, the two-in-three figure might not directly translate to the UK population. Currently, around 13% of Australian adults smoke, whereas in the UK, this figure stands at approximately 20%.

Quitting smoking can substantially reduce an individual's health risks. NHS Smokefree states that a decade after cessation, the risk of lung cancer halves compared to continuing smokers, and the risk of heart attack becomes comparable to that of a non-smoker.

374 workers were made redundant after Tullis Russell Papermakers, located in Markinch, Fife, entered administration in April 2015. Subsequently, each affected individual was awarded eight weeks' pay as compensation. This settlement came after a ruling by an employment tribunal in Dundee.

According to legal representatives, the company directors failed to meet their legal duty to give at least 45 days' notice, a requirement when over 100 staff are made redundant. This neglect meant that every employee had grounds to pursue compensation. Nevertheless, individual claims to the employment tribunal would have been "extremely complex" and costly for each worker, leading them to collectively pursue the claim.

David Martyn, a senior employment solicitor from Thompsons, the firm representing the former employees, commented: "The more preparation time employees have before such significant changes, the better equipped they are to manage their finances and lessen the impact. This compensation payout will be covered by the UK's administration service. Consequently, taxpayers are bearing the cost due to the directors' disregard for regulations. This practice must cease, and I believe stronger criminal charges should be brought against companies acting in this manner."

The Old Bailey trial revealed that the assailant, having dismounted a stolen moped, stabbed Appleton with a 25-inch (63cm) serrated knife. The 17-year-old attacker, whose identity is protected by law due to his age, was acquitted of murder but is scheduled for sentencing on April 21. Jurors heard that Appleton, an Islington college student, was with companions when his attacker dismounted a scooter, produced the weapon, and pursued the group. After tripping and falling, Appleton was repeatedly stabbed. Police confirmed his death resulted from shock and haemorrhage caused by a chest stab wound. The Metropolitan Police has since issued warnings about 'zombie' knives, noting how these decorative blades are being marketed. The force also highlighted that children were present and playing in the park during the incident. As the killer was driven away from the scene, the court was told he yelled "RP," short for Red Pitch, signifying a rival gang to one in Nightingale Park. The 17-year-old alleged getaway driver was also acquitted of murder, and another 17-year-old boy was found not guilty of conspiring to inflict grievous bodily harm. Following the machete attack, the assailant escaped to Bristol, attempting to fly to Malaga, Spain, but was apprehended upon his return to London, where he sought to evade capture. The killer's defence claimed he had been attacked while trying to retrieve his stolen bicycle from another boy. The court also heard of his previous conviction for blade possession, having been caught with a lock-knife in a McDonald's restaurant a year prior to the killing. Prosecutor Simon Denison QC lamented Appleton's death as yet "another tragic waste of a young life" lost to knife violence. Firstly, a significant portion of the sale price – three-quarters of a billion pounds – is allocated not for manufacturing plants, but for loans taken out by Opel and Vauxhall car owners through GM's financial services division. Peugeot is acquiring these outstanding loans at eighty percent of their book value.

Secondly, GM will retain the majority of the existing pension liabilities. Peugeot will assume responsibility for a few specific schemes, for which GM is paying them £2.6 billion as an agreement fee.

Thirdly, the Detroit-based automotive giant will record an accounting impairment of £3.2 billion on the transaction. This confirms that the valuation it previously held for Opel and Vauxhall in its own financial records was largely driven by optimism and the scale of past investments, rather than concrete expectations of future profits.

However, GM's financial outlay does not imply that Vauxhall and Opel are destined not to succeed under their new owner. Peugeot anticipates generating £1.5 billion in cost savings from the integrated operations, and should the deal help the French automaker penetrate new markets, it will have served its purpose.

Meanwhile, GM continues to scale back its global ambitions and sharpen its strategic focus. Since receiving a bailout from the US government following the financial crisis, it has discontinued American brands such as Oldsmobile, Saturn, Hummer, and Pontiac, and divested its Australian plants, which had produced cars since 1931.

This strategic retraction might be perceived as a departure from former prominence, but it could also reflect GM's pragmatic conviction that its future lies in China – where it is the most robust US competitor – and in electric and self-driving vehicles, sectors where America, not Europe, holds a leadership position.

A Royal Air Force plane from the Rhodesian Squadron, stationed at RAF Wittering, crashed in Holme on November 22, 1940. Pilot Officer Harold Penketh, a Brighton native, tragically died without bailing out. The aircraft's remains, identified as a Spitfire, were discovered following a geophysical survey of the site. There is an expectation that the salvaged components will eventually be exhibited publicly. Although the precise cause of the crash was never definitively determined, eyewitnesses reported that the Mk 1A Spitfire, serial number X4583, broke away from its formation and plunged nose-first into agricultural land in the village of Holme, located south of Peterborough. An investigation concluded that either the pilot's oxygen supply system failed or the aircraft itself experienced a structural malfunction. The 20-year-old Pilot Officer Penketh apparently made no attempt to deploy his parachute. His body was recovered from the debris and subsequently returned to his relatives. John Bliss, an eyewitness who was a child at the time, recounted that the "enormous crater" formed by the Spitfire's impact rapidly filled with water due to the area's high water table. For 75 years, the Spitfire's wreckage lay submerged in its watery resting place. Cranfield University successfully located the crash site in August, using a combination of a geophysical survey and metal detection. The excavation, commencing on Monday and anticipated to last a week, is being overseen by Oxford Archaeology East. The retrieved components, which remain the property of the Ministry of Defence, will undergo cleaning and documentation. Portions of them are slated for public exhibition later this month. Private Sean Benton was discovered deceased at the Deepcut barracks in Surrey in June 1995, having sustained five gunshot wounds while on guard duty at a perimeter fence. The human rights group Liberty stated that the Attorney General has granted his family permission to apply to the High Court, despite an earlier inquest having recorded a suicide verdict for the 20-year-old soldier.

Earlier this month, a second inquest, examining the death of Private Cheryl James – who also died at Deepcut in 1995 from a single gunshot wound – similarly returned a suicide verdict. Over 100 witnesses testified during the Cheryl James inquiry. In his ruling, Coroner Brian Barker QC strongly criticized Deepcut's welfare provisions, citing compelling evidence of a pervasive sexualized environment.

Representing Pte Benton's twin brother Tony and his sister Tracy Lewis, Liberty submitted an application to the Attorney General in July 2015, seeking to nullify the initial July 1995 inquest and demand a new investigation. Liberty stated that since Pte Benton's death, numerous individuals have informed his family and publicly asserted their belief that he, originally from Hastings, East Sussex, endured physical and psychological bullying at the barracks.

Ms Lewis expressed being "overwhelmed and disturbed by all the details of the shameful environment at Deepcut which have finally come to light through the Cheryl James inquest – it is terrible to think of Sean alone there." She added that over two decades after their brother's passing, and having recently lost both parents, she and Tony are "determined to find out what happened to Sean."

Pte Benton was the initial casualty among four young recruits who succumbed to gunshot wounds at Deepcut between 1995 and 2002. Liberty highlighted that the first inquest, held merely a month after his death, involved testimony from only six individuals. Crucially, Pte Benton's medical and mental health records were not procured, nor was any evidence gathered or presented regarding his experiences at the barracks. Emma Norton, a lawyer for Liberty, asserted that a proper and independent investigation into Pte Benton's death in 1995 could have spared his family decades of suffering and unresolved questions.

Early telemetry received after Tuesday's high-speed flyby of the icy dwarf planet (14 km/s or 31,000 mph) confirmed the New Horizons spacecraft remained stable and encountered no problems. This crucial signal was relayed through a large communication antenna located in Madrid, Spain, part of NASA's global network. Traveling across 4.7 billion kilometers of space, the message required four hours and 25 minutes to reach Earth.

Anticipation grew among scientists and engineers at mission control in Laurel, Maryland, as they awaited the vital telemetry. Consequently, immense joy and relief erupted at 01:52 BST when the signal finally arrived, prompting team members to cheer, embrace, and wave American flags in celebration. "We are in lock with telemetry from the spacecraft," announced Alice Bowman, the mission operations manager, upon confirmation of the signal. She added, "We have a healthy spacecraft, we have recorded data from the Pluto system, and we are outbound from Pluto." Minutes later, she conveyed her profound satisfaction, stating, "I can't express how I feel. It's just like we planned it!"

NASA Administrator Charles Bolden remarked that "With this mission, we have visited every single planet in the Solar System," highlighting a significant milestone. John Grunsfeld, the agency's science chief, described the event as "a tremendous moment in human history," further expressing anticipation for the spacecraft's data, which he noted was "full of images and we can't wait."

Alice Bowman, the operations manager, affirmed that New Horizons' solid-state recorder was indeed filled with data. She clarified, "The expected number of segments on that recorder had been used. That tells us that that data has been collected on the spacecraft." The initial signal received Wednesday morning consisted solely of engineering data, intended to verify the successful execution of the flyby sequence. High-resolution images from the encounter were expected to be downlinked later that same day.

Ralph Semmel, director of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, the home of mission control, extended congratulations to the entire mission team. He humorously noted Pluto's offerings: "Whales, doughnuts, and a heart," referring to the informal monikers given to surface features visible in images captured during the spacecraft's approach.

Despite the team's confidence in a successful flyby, there remained a slight risk that New Horizons could be lost while traversing the Pluto system at high speed. A collision with even minute icy debris at its velocity of 14 km/s would have proven fatal to the spacecraft. To mark the occasion, James Christy, discoverer of Pluto's moon Charon, and relatives of Clyde Tombaugh, who discovered the dwarf planet in 1930, gathered at mission control to witness the signal's arrival.

Parliament has, for the first time, formally endorsed the commencement of the UK's departure from the EU by March's end following a vote by MPs. The government's chief whip appeared visibly pleased after the night's proceedings. This ministerial concession was, however, strategically astute; it secured Labour's support for the Article 50 activation timeline with only a nebulous pledge of a future plan, potentially as insubstantial as a brief scribble.

However, discontent simmers within Labour ranks regarding the handling of the issue, with reports of angry exchanges, suggesting some feel their leadership was outmaneuvered by the government's scheme. Pro-Remain Conservative dissenters remain highly skeptical of the government's underlying motives for providing further details on its Brexit strategy. Though they retreated today, their challenge is far from over.

Yet, beyond these immediate political maneuvers and the whip's evident satisfaction, the past 24 hours have underscored two crucial realities. Firstly, the vote's outcome indicates that very few MPs intend to outright obstruct Brexit or impede the process. While they will undoubtedly press the government for greater specificity and seek to modify any eventual proposals reaching the Commons, potentially causing disruption or delays, halting the departure entirely is not the objective for most.

Secondly, it's equally apparent that Prime Minister Theresa May lacks a stable majority on EU matters. Once her detailed plans are finally presented to Parliament, she will almost certainly be compelled to make concessions. This explains the government's strenuous efforts in the Supreme Court to prevent parliamentary intervention before complex negotiations in Brussels even commence.

He had previously alleged that the campaign was plagued by internal disputes. Reports indicated he was close to resigning in February when Labour MP Kate Hoey joined a competing "out" group.

In his letter of resignation, the home shopping executive explained his belief that a robust and independent Labour perspective advocating for leaving the EU would prove more beneficial and effective for the Leave campaign. He noted that he could now fully devote himself to his role as director of Labour Leave, thereby cultivating that distinct voice. He added that, leading up to the 23 June vote, Labour Leave intended to present a powerful and well-reasoned left-of-centre case for Britain's exit from the EU.

The overwhelming majority of Labour Members of Parliament favor Britain remaining within the EU, with only approximately twelve actively campaigning for departure. Former Labour minister Frank Field cautioned the party that its stance on remaining in the EU risked alienating a significant number of voters, potentially losing them to UKIP. Mr. Mills, who played a key role in the 1975 referendum campaign against European Economic Community membership, has also expressed disapproval of Jeremy Corbyn's decision to support staying in.

Mr. Mills voiced his hope that his choice would be a transformative initial step in encouraging Labour supporters, who are still undecided, to vote Leave in June to secure a better, fairer future for the country. He also stated that Labour Leave would continue its collaboration with Vote Leave, as well as other pro-exit campaigns across the spectrum, to ensure a stronger future for the UK outside the EU.

Vote Leave was the organization chosen by the Electoral Commission to spearhead the argument for Britain's withdrawal from the European Union. It is led by prominent Conservative figures Boris Johnson and Michael Gove, alongside Labour MP Gisela Stuart, and receives backing from Liberal Democrat and UKIP personalities, as well as business professionals.

Rehtaeh Parsons, a 17-year-old from Nova Scotia, took her own life in April after enduring relentless torment stemming from a photograph of her alleged rape by four boys, as reported by her mother. In connection with this image, two 18-year-old men were apprehended on Thursday. These individuals, whose identities remain undisclosed, are slated to face legal proceedings in a juvenile court.

Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) Chief Superintendent Roland Wells, from the Halifax district, released a statement Thursday evening expressing hope that these arrests would aid in the community's healing process. He remarked, "A young girl has died in what was a tragic set of circumstances. We all need to reflect on how we as a community can come together in Rehtaeh's memory and see what we can do to work together to support our youth."

Regarding the charges, one of the men faces two counts related to the distribution of child pornography. The other individual has been charged with a single count each of creating child pornography and distributing child pornography. The RCMP clarified that the names of the accused would not be disclosed because they were legally considered youths at the time of the alleged offense. The police further cautioned Halifax residents against publicly revealing the accused's identities, warning of potential prosecution, and advised against any vigilante actions.

According to Rehtaeh's mother, Leah Parsons, her daughter attended a party in 2011 at the age of 15, where she became heavily intoxicated after consuming vodka. Rehtaeh confided in her parents that while severely inebriated, she was raped by four boys, and a photograph of the incident was taken. This image subsequently circulated online, leading to incessant bullying from her schoolmates. "She was never left alone," Ms Parsons informed CBC News in April following Rehtaeh's suicide. She elaborated that Rehtaeh's friends abandoned her, she faced constant harassment, and unknown boys began contacting her via text and Facebook, propositioning her for sex given her alleged history with their friends. "It just never stopped," her mother recounted.

Rehtaeh passed away in April in the hospital, several days after her suicide attempt. Initially, police stated there were insufficient grounds for arrests concerning either the alleged rape or the photograph. However, the investigation was reopened in April after new information came to light.

Morrisons, a supermarket chain, sold My Local to Greybull Capital last year and has since committed to offering positions to former My Local employees. The retailer found it difficult to compete in the fiercely competitive and price-war-ridden grocery market.

Formerly known as Morrisons' M Local, My Local was acquired by Greybull for £25 million. This acquisition was spearheaded by Mike Greene, an experienced figure in retail who gained public recognition from his appearance on Channel 4's The Secret Millionaire.

My Local had indicated earlier this month that administrators were alerted to assume control of the business. Just last week, Morrisons extended a helping hand to My Local's staff, proposing job opportunities within its own supermarkets in the event of store closures.

Mike Greene expressed his regret, stating that the past nine months constituted "one of the toughest retail trading periods" he had ever encountered, with My Local confronting "intense competition." He added that the management team was "unable to return the business to profitability," for which he was "truly sorry."

Mark Orton, a partner at KPMG and joint administrator, commented that the management faced "tough trading conditions," and despite their "best efforts to improve performance," My Local ultimately "was unable to return to viability." He confirmed that while most stores have now ceased operations, KPMG is engaged in "active discussions with a number of interested parties" regarding both the 32 remaining operational premises and a select few that have already shut down.

Daniela Comelli, the study's lead author, stated that "a significant nickel content unequivocally points to meteoritic iron." According to the researchers, ancient Egyptians highly valued meteoritic iron, frequently using it for crafting exquisite ornamental or ceremonial items. Their findings indicate that Egyptians in the 13th century BCE already recognized that these unusual iron fragments descended from the heavens, a realization that predated Western understanding by over two millennia. The blade's superior craftsmanship, especially when contrasted with simpler meteoritic iron artifacts, "implies a remarkable proficiency in ironworking during Tutankhamun's reign," the team noted. South Korea's shipping and shipbuilding industries are among those most severely impacted by a prolonged global trade downturn. A decline in orders has resulted in overcapacity, suppressed freight rates, and an escalation of debts. Nomura analyst Young Sun Kwon explained that Korean shipping companies have suffered substantial losses primarily because charter rates for leased vessels were fixed at high levels in 2010, while actual shipping rates have subsequently fallen.

The South Korean government is now preparing to implement a difficult, industry-wide restructuring, which will necessitate significant job cuts. Krystal Tan from Capital Economics stated that this ongoing restructuring is one reason why weak economic growth is anticipated this year and next. She added that the loss of tens of thousands of jobs would certainly negatively affect economic sentiment. The 26-year-old full-back originally departed the Blues for France in summer 2014. According to Pivac, any returning Welsh player, including Halfpenny, would be considered for discussions if they are serious about coming back to Wales. He emphasized that while budgets are not limitless, the club is always interested in speaking with Welsh players re-entering the market to ascertain their availability and worth.

Should the 2013 British and Irish Lions full-back return to Wales, it would likely be via a national dual contract, with the Welsh Rugby Union contributing 60% of the funding. Under the standing agreement between the WRU and the four Welsh regions, the player's former region is granted the first opportunity to re-sign them, which positions the Blues as the probable frontrunners. However, this protocol isn't absolute, as demonstrated by flanker Dan Lydiate, who chose to join Ospreys instead of his former club, Newport Gwent Dragons, upon his return from Racing 92.

Another significant consideration for Halfpenny could be joining a region that has secured a spot in the 2016-17 European Champions Cup. This season, Scarlets and Ospreys represent Wales in the competition, while the Blues would need to significantly improve their Pro12 performance to qualify for the subsequent season. Given Halfpenny's triumph in the tournament with Toulon last season, participating in Europe's elite club competition could prove a strong incentive.

Following his team's 20-12 Pro12 victory over Zebre, Pivac further stated Scarlets' strong desire to retain club captain Scott Williams. The Welsh international centre, who like Halfpenny is currently recovering from surgery, is on a dual contract set to expire in summer 2016. Pivac expressed hope that Williams would return to play before his contract concludes, adding that while many discussions are underway internally, he couldn't disclose information beyond what was publicly available. This most northerly Orkney island is home to only around 50 residents. Orkney Islands Council stated the school would resume operation if additional families with young children relocate to the island. The facility also serves as a hub for local community groups. Island inhabitants attribute the scarcity of young families to inadequate transport connections. Teigan expressed to the BBC her excitement for secondary school but conveyed apprehension regarding her former school's future. "I'm eager to attend the larger school," she remarked. "However, a slight sadness lingers because the school's closure makes me fear the island could decline."

Councillor Kevin Woodbridge noted that North Ronaldsay's population has halved since his arrival in 1977. He commented, "It's deeply saddening, yet it illustrates the island's decline that has culminated in this situation." "When I first came, there were 17 pupils at the school and 127 residents on the island; now, the population stands at 50 to 60." He added, "The standard of living on the island could be significantly enhanced."

Billy Muir, who chairs the community council, described losing the school's sole pupil as "a severe setback for the community that will undoubtedly trigger wider consequences." He stated, "We require new housing to be constructed and new families to move in. A school needs several children, not just one." "Faster broadband is also essential." "There's no sense in sugar-coating things; we must be pragmatic. Hopefully, this situation draws attention to our predicament."

A spokesperson for the local authority explained: "The single classroom at North Ronaldsay Primary School is located within a building that accommodates various community amenities. The classroom will remain on standby from August and would be reactivated for educational use should families with primary-aged children relocate to the island. Meanwhile, it will stay accessible to all North Ronaldsay residents for various learning activities, overseen by the local community association. This strategy for keeping the room actively utilized was developed through discussions between Orkney Islands Council and several North Ronaldsay community groups."

At 88 years old, Hank Costain, a resident of Charminster near Dorchester, made his inaugural Spitfire flight in 1942, when he was just 19. The Supermarine Spitfire itself had its first flight from Eastleigh Aerodrome (now Southampton Airport) on March 5, 1936. Mr. Costain fondly recalled flying the Spitfire, calling the experience "absolutely marvellous." He elaborated, stating that the initial acceleration upon engaging the throttle felt like a powerful push, launching the aircraft forward instantly. The aircraft was incredibly responsive, he noted, describing its controls as lighter than other planes, allowing for rapid acceleration and effortless aerobatic maneuvers. However, he stressed the need for careful handling: "Treat a Spitfire well, and it would reciprocate; mishandle it or be negligent, and you'd face problems like ground looping." He also highlighted its delicate landing gear, prone to collapse.

Mr. Costain served in the Royal Air Force for 37 years. His combat flights in Spitfires spanned numerous regions, including Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, and Burma. During his service, he also trained others as a Spitfire instructor and later became a test pilot for the aircraft at 9MU Cosford, Shropshire. According to him, the Spitfire was highly coveted: "Every air force recruit dreamed of flying a Spitfire." He proudly claimed to have piloted "nearly all of the operational Spitfire variants," adding, "Few people remain who have experienced as many different Spitfire marks as I have."

Mr. Costain frequently fielded questions, both during and after his flying career, about whether he experienced fear during the war. He admitted, "I was terrified," but clarified his fear was primarily of "letting my friends see" his apprehension, leading him to resolve never to show it. Ashley Broomhall recently completed challenging mountain climbs, first scaling 3,560ft (1,085m) Snowdon in Snowdonia before undertaking the 4,406ft (1,344m) Ben Nevis near Fort William, Scotland. The ascent and descent of Ben Nevis took him seven hours. He now plans to hike 3,208ft (978m) Scafell Pike in the Lake District.

Mr. Broomhall, a 28-year-old from Whitchurch in Shropshire, is tackling these peaks to generate funds for Cancer Research UK, a personal mission inspired by his mother's cancer diagnosis. For over five years, he has been a member of the 501st UK Garrison, a Star Wars costuming club whose members attend events across the UK in "movie-accurate" outfits to raise money for various charities.

For his summer ascents of Snowdon and Ben Nevis, Mr. Broomhall adapted his Imperial stormtrooper costume for improved flexibility during the climbs. Prioritizing safety, he opted for regular walking boots instead of his costume footwear, which was unsuitable for the demanding terrain, and was accompanied by friends.

While climbing Ben Nevis, Scotland's highest Munro and Britain's tallest mountain, dressed as a stormtrooper and proudly carrying a UK Garrison flag, Mr. Broomhall garnered significant attention. He noted that other climbers were often bewildered by the sight of a stormtrooper on the mountain, an unexpected encounter. He handed out cards explaining his purpose, receiving enthusiastic support and donations from fellow trekkers.

Higher on Ben Nevis, he navigated through sections of thigh-deep snow. At one of these snowy expanses, he and his walking companion engaged in a playful snowball fight with other hikers. Upon reaching the final snowfield that led to the summit, Mr. Broomhall described a surge of pride as he charged forward with the flag. Greeted by cheers from climbers already there, he triumphantly planted his flag, symbolically claiming the summit for the "Empire." He expressed his enjoyment of the challenge and his affection for Scotland and its Munros, declaring his intention to conquer Scafell Pike also in his distinctive armour, having successfully done so for the first two peaks.

During the Blackpool Town Hall hearing, it was revealed that Miss Percival, who has special educational needs, sought a pregnancy termination at her GP surgery in August 2014. However, the procedure could not be performed as her pregnancy was too advanced. She admitted to having avoided confronting her pregnancy and to having concealed it from her parents due to fear of their response.

Mr. Percival, then the vicar of Holy Trinity CE Church in Freckleton, recounted that on the afternoon of November 25, upon her return from work, she spent time in the downstairs restroom. He described seeing her emerge from the bathroom around 3:30 PM GMT, carrying a towel he thought was soiled with excrement. They went outside to dispose of it when, he stated, "Jonathan's leg came into view." He testified in court, recalling his words to Ruth: "This is a baby, you can't put a baby in the bin." He then stated he laid the infant on the towel on the ground outside and tried to revive him. He described the baby as "extremely cold, completely lifeless," concluding, "The baby was clearly deceased."

Medical evidence presented at the inquest indicated the baby was alive at birth. Miss Percival testified that she believed she saw the baby attempt to breathe, yet also stated, "I somehow thought I had a miscarriage because, to me, the baby was dead when it emerged from me." Previously unreleased archive footage brings together a vibrant tapestry of Ulster's past, showcasing events from Winston Churchill's notable Belfast visit in 1912 and a 1963 Viking re-enactment in a County Down coastal town, alongside stories of tourism, industrial legacy, and athletic endeavors. As part of a significant historical initiative called 'From Britain On Film', the British Film Institute (BFI) has made hundreds of previously unreleased films from its archives available for public online viewing at no cost. The collection chronicles royal tours and civic parades, including Churchill's 1912 speech at Belfast's Celtic Park, where he spoke to nationalists and endorsed Home Rule. Additionally, numerous travel films are featured, originally designed to promote Northern Ireland as a tourist destination to audiences in Great Britain and the United States, thereby boosting visitor numbers prior to the onset of the Troubles. The archive also highlights sporting events, such as the 1930 Ulster Tourist Trophy race, held at the Ards circuit in County Down, an event that drew thousands of onlookers and captivated the international motorsport community.

However, the most compelling material lies in the footage depicting everyday individuals engaged in remarkable activities. Scenes of workers in spinning mills and the construction of the M1 motorway at Stockman's Lane in Belfast showcase Northern Ireland's industrial peak. One film documents Northern Ireland's inaugural hosting of the World Ploughing Championships, where, appropriately, a local competitor claimed victory. This 1959 competition in Armoy, County Antrim, is preserved in colour footage, capturing Lawrence McMillan's triumphant moment as he secured the Golden Plough.

Yet, a 1938 recording from Belfast's Royal Victoria Hospital proves arguably the most insightful. It offers an uncommon look into its casualty department and operating theatres as they operated a decade before the National Health Service was established. While medical practices have progressed significantly over the subsequent eighty years, certain aspects of healthcare in Northern Ireland seem to persist; the film concludes with the hospital's management board chairman appealing for reduced waiting lists.

Francis Jones of Northern Ireland Screen, responsible for collecting much of this material, stated that the project's goal was to safeguard fragile films that were at risk of deterioration or loss. He added that film possesses a unique nostalgic value, distinct from engaging with textbooks or history books. "Witnessing the footage firsthand offers a visceral connection that truly resonates with viewers," he commented. The entire 'From Britain On Film' archive is accessible via the BFI Player.

RamJam recently launched 'Southern Rail Tycoon' on Thursday, attracting 45,000 players to its satirical gameplay. In this light-hearted game, the objective is to prevent guards from boarding trains. Succeeding in this leads to service cancellations, from which players 'profit' by collecting virtual fares. The game draws its inspiration from the persistent train cancellations experienced over recent months, a result of an ongoing dispute with the RMT union. Players lose when a sufficient number of guards successfully board a train, causing the delayed service to finally depart.

Tom Jackson, a developer based in Brighton, shared his personal frustration, recounting how a planned trip to London a month prior was repeatedly delayed and then ultimately cancelled, leading his group to abandon train travel altogether. This frustrating experience prompted Mr. Jackson and his colleagues, Phil Hart and Toby Funnell, to create the game. The 39-year-old developer explained that the game serves a dual purpose: offering a fun distraction for commuters enduring train delays and raising awareness about the available compensation policies. Upon game completion, links are provided to Southern Rail's official compensation page and their Twitter account.

Jackson further elaborated that their studio enjoys creating games that are "reactive" to current events, demonstrating the "impact" news has on individuals. He described the train service as "an absolute shambles" and "incredibly frustrating".

A spokesperson for Southern Rail countered, stating that cancelling trains actually results in financial losses for them. They expressed efforts to provide the "best service possible under very difficult circumstances" and offered a "sincere apology".

The root of the ongoing issue lies in a dispute between the RMT union and GTR concerning the proposed increase in driver-only operated (DOO) services, which would alter the responsibilities of conductors. Due to regular strikes, Southern cancelled 341 daily train services on July 11, citing a need to improve "reliability." Since then, 15 of these services have been reinstated.

The continuous delays on the line, managed by Govia Thameslink Railway, led to the resignation of Rail Minister Claire Perry last Friday. The new Transport Secretary, Chris Grayling, declared on Monday that resolving the strike action was "top of his priority list".

Professor Duncan Wingham stated that the controversy surrounding the name had "put a smile" on people's faces. However, Members of Parliament questioned if ministers, who ultimately named the ship after Sir David Attenborough, would consequently punish Professor Wingham.

Wingham was providing testimony to the Commons Science and Technology Committee regarding this highly publicized event, which generated immense public interest and divided opinion after "Boaty McBoatface" was overlooked for the main ship. He characterized the ministers' resolution to christen the primary vessel after the renowned zoologist and broadcaster – an option that ranked fourth in the survey – while also assigning "Boaty McBoatface" to a remotely operated sub-sea vehicle, as an "eloquent compromise."

When Conservative MP Nicola Blackwood asked about the episode's impact on public engagement in science, Wingham, an academic, asserted that the "extraordinary attention" it garnered could only be seen as an "incredible success." He proclaimed that NERC could now "make the claim that we are probably the best-known research council in the world." He further added that, as a result, "hundreds of thousands of people, not only in the UK but around the world," now know about NERC and its scientific work. Wingham concluded, "In many ways we feel this has been an astonishingly great outcome for us. In addition, it has put a smile on everyone's face."
